SHANGHAI
FEB. 23, 1933
Dear Eat Orbs.
You have the weather to thank, or blame, for this letter. I started to go
out to see the movie Grand Hotel which I have always missed at St. Louis, New York
Bolton and other American metropolitan centers, but when I got ready to call one of
the many Richsha boys the rain was coming down in torrents, so decided to stay in
my room. My night boy was much relieved when I came back - he tried to tell me that
the rain was coming down in bucket fulls be fore I went out - but all I could make
out of his conversation was "Master no go, velly bad lain, catchy cold". Didn't make
up my mind as to what he had said until later - his talk was not as plain as it looks
in print. He is always most solicitous about me and gives me such service as you
have never known. The Hotel requests that tips be within reason and
five cents, our money, per day. They probably have to do a lot of educating to get
good boys - the "boys"
"boys" will retire if the guests get liberal. Everyother word with them is "Catchy".
"Shall Master catchy bath, or catchy bleakfast, catchy laundry, etc. "They never get
an "r". You get so used to saying "more big" and "more high" and such "Pigeon" talk
that its very hard to keep those expressions out of your ordinary conversation with
other people not Chinese.
It is quite easy to get around wherever you want to go without knowing
any Chinese. Almost all of them here in Shanghai speak some English, at least enough
to direct you.
Have given up all idea, if I ever had any, of trying to learn their
language. The written characters are the same all over China, but the spoken words
are entirely different in sound. For instance the numeral Three is pronounced "Sam"
in Canton, and "Sen" in Shanghai. Two is "Liang" in Shanghai, and "Ye" in Canton.
So a man from Canton might as well be in Germany as here, so far as making himself
understood is concerned, unless he knows how to write. This is one reason for their
lack of unity, but a more important factor is the fact that a mans family come first
followed by his city, then by his province and last the nation. One of the men I
have met here told me of having dined with a Chinese woman the night before. She had
been educated abroad and spoke English perfectly. During the course of the dinner
he asked her where she was from in China and she told him the name of a small town
in one of the Southern provinces. He remarked that she did not use the dialect of
that district, and she exclaimed "Oh my family left there two hundred years ago". He
admitted that
was an extreme case because she was very proud of her ancestry, but
said that he had run across innumerable cases where the man or woman had never seen
their"home" as they called it. The Chinese who leave for other countries seem to
develop a rather keen love for the "Fatherland" but that is not true of those who
stay home. This fact has misled a lot of people in the United States and elsewhere
to expect a lot more National cooperation in the Jehol area than will probably be
forthcoming. I do hope there may be some way out of that threatened calamity. Wrote
to Walter Weisenburger yesterday and told him that he probably knew more about what
was going on over here through the St. Louis Press than I do - unless he says "star"
instead of "Paper"
Ine field for Aviation is apparently almost unlimited because of the lack
of transportation facilities between large centers of population. Most travel is by
water,
the service is infrequent, extremely slow and schedules poorly maintained.
There is a tremendous interest in Airtransport but they seem to know very little
centuries, controlled by availability of water transportation. The necessity of buy-
ing equipment wich gold and paying for it in depreciated silor is bas.
